before: Aarav looks around the room and thinks: everyone here is eating something different. Everyone here is hungry at the same time, and everyone will feel better in ten minutes.
after: Aarav looks around the room: the lunches differ. Which ingredients do they share, and what does the body obtain from them?

before: You will almost certainly find both. Some foods — rice or wheat, dal, milk, oil, salt, sugar — turn up in nearly every diary in the class. Others turn up in one diary only, because one family cooks that dish and the others do not.
after: Your diaries may share ingredients, but check rather than assume this. A food absent from four diaries may appear in another household. Four diaries cannot represent the whole class or region.

before: If a single classroom holds this much variety, country of this size holds far more. A traveller who ate breakfast in Amritsar, lunch in Bengaluru and dinner in Imphal would eat three meals with almost nothing in common.
after: A traveller eating in Amritsar, Bengaluru and Imphal could find different dishes and shared ingredients. A regional label does not describe every household. Compare examples before generalising.

before: The relationship is hard to miss. Punjab grows wheat, and Punjabi food is built on wheat. Karnataka grows ragi, and ragi appears in Karnataka's everyday meals. Manipur grows rice and bamboo, and both turn up on the Manipuri plate.
after: The examples link wheat with Punjabi dishes, ragi with dishes in Karnataka, and rice with dishes in Manipur. Is the same relationship present in your other rows? Look for an exception as well.

before: This makes sense once you think about where food has to travel from. For most of human history, and for most families even today, the cheapest and freshest food is the food grown nearby. A cuisine is, in large part, a set of clever answers to the question: what can we cook with what grows here?
after: Local crops can influence food traditions, but proximity alone does not guarantee the cheapest or freshest food. Transport, storage, season and farming costs also matter.

before: And what grows here depends on two things a farmer cannot choose — the soil and the climate. Rice needs standing water and warmth. Ragi tolerates poor soil and low rainfall. Mustard grows in cool northern winters. India has an unusual range of soils and climates, which is exactly why it has an unusual range of food.
after: Soil, rainfall and temperature affect which crops grow well. Rice is often grown in flooded fields, though not all rice requires standing water. Ragi can tolerate relatively dry conditions. Farmers can also change irrigation and soil management.

before: so regional food is explained by cultivation, and then modified by taste, culture and tradition.
after: Regional food reflects crops, trade, cost, taste, culture and tradition. A crops-and-dishes table suggests relationships; it does not isolate a single cause.

before: Name one dish that is eaten in your state but not in the state next to it. What grows in your state that might explain it?
after: Choose a dish common in your state. Is it also eaten across the border? Check with two sources before explaining any difference using crops, trade or tradition.

before: Food varies across the map. Does it also vary across the years? Ask the oldest person you can reach, and you will find that it does — not just the dishes, but the whole business of cooking. The tools have changed, the fuel has changed, the time it takes has changed.
after: Food varies across the map. Does it also vary across the years? Interview an older person about dishes, fuel and cooking tools. Record continuity as well as change; one memory cannot represent every household.

before: Fifty years ago most Indian households cooked over a chulha burning wood, dung cakes or coal (Fig. 3.1 a). Someone had to gather the fuel, light the fire, and tend it. Today most households cook on a gas stove that lights in one second and goes out in one second (Fig. 3.1b). Spices and grain were once ground by hand on a sil-batta, a heavy stone slab worked with a stone roller (Fig. 3.1 c). Now a mixer-grinder does the same work in a minute (Fig. 3.1d).
after: A chulha burns fuel such as wood or dung cakes; a gas stove burns gas. A sil-batta grinds food by hand; a mixer-grinder uses an electric motor. These tools coexist today. Your interviews can show which changes occurred in particular homes and when.

before: And partly because communication changed. Recipes now travel by television, phone and internet. A dish that belonged to one region for three hundred years can spread across the country in a season.
after: Television, phones and the internet can spread recipes beyond a region. To test a claim about how quickly one dish spread, we would need dated evidence from several places.

before: It also brings losses. Some traditional grains and dishes are disappearing, and with them the knowledge of how to cook them. Some of those grains, as we will see later in this chapter, were more nourishing than what replaced them.
after: Changes can also reduce the use of familiar grains or cooking skills. Whether a replacement is more nourishing depends on its ingredients, preparation and quantity. Compare examples rather than assuming that older or newer food is better.

before: Aarav skips breakfast on Wednesday. By the second period he cannot follow what the teacher is saying, and by the third his hands feel unsteady. At break, Ira gives him half a banana. Within a few minutes he feels roughly human again.
after: Aarav misses breakfast and feels hungry during class. Ira shares a banana at break. Later he says he feels better.

before: Half a banana. A few minutes. Something in that banana reached his blood fast enough to change how he felt in class.
after: Does that observation prove what caused the change? Rest, water and other factors may matter too. We need knowledge of digestion to explain what food can supply; this story is not a blood-sugar test.

before: Start with the component that rescued Aarav.
after: Begin with carbohydrates, one group of food components.

before: Glucose is the simplest sugar the body runs on, and it is a carbohydrate. Carbohydrates are the body's main source of quick energy. This is why a marathon runner drinks glucose water during a race rather than eating a meal: glucose needs almost no processing before the muscles can use it.
after: Glucose is a simple sugar and a carbohydrate. Cells can release energy from glucose. Starch is also a carbohydrate; digestion breaks it down into smaller sugars before absorption. Foods supply mixtures, so a banana is not a dose of pure glucose.

before: In winter, many Indian households make laddoos. The reason is not only that they taste good. A laddoo is built from flour, ghee, goond, nuts and seeds. Ghee is a fat, and so are the cooking oils in every Indian kitchen — groundnut, mustard, coconut, sunflower, soya bean, sesame. Fats do the same essential job as carbohydrates — they supply energy — but they do it differently. Gram for gram, fat carries more than twice the energy of carbohydrate, and the body stores it rather than burning it at once. Fat is stored energy: the reserve the body draws on when food is not coming in, and part of how it keeps warm. That is why a laddoo belongs to winter. It is dense, slow energy at the time of year the body needs most of it.
after: Ghee and cooking oils contain fats. Fat supplies about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrate. The body can use fat for energy or store it; it does not automatically store all dietary fat. Stored fat also cushions organs and reduces heat loss. These functions do not establish a special need for laddoos in winter.

before: The bear that does not eat for months Before winter, a polar bear eats heavily and builds a thick layer of fat under its skin. Through the long winter it may eat almost nothing, living off that stored fat while the same layer keeps it warm. Stored fat is a survival strategy, not a flaw — which is worth remembering before deciding that all fat is bad.
after: Stored fat in a polar bear: pregnant females can spend months in a den without feeding, drawing on stored reserves while giving birth and nursing cubs. Most other polar bears remain active and hunt through winter. Fat also provides insulation.

before: Carbohydrates and fats keep a body running. Neither one builds it.
after: Carbohydrates and fats supply energy, and fats also form parts of cells. Proteins have an essential role in building and repairing tissues. These job labels overlap; they are not exclusive compartments.

before: Plant sources of protein include all pulses — moong, tuar dal, gram, kidney beans, peas — along with soya bean, groundnut and other nuts and seeds. Animal sources include milk, curd, paneer, cheese, egg, fish, chicken and meat. Edible mushrooms are a good source too.
after: Pulses, soya beans, nuts and seeds supply protein. Milk, curd, paneer, eggs, fish and meat are other sources. Compare amounts as well as presence: fresh mushrooms contain protein but are mostly water and supply less per usual serving than pulses.

before: Mushrooms Mushrooms are not plants. They belong to a separate group of living things — fungi — and they grow in dark, damp places without sunlight. Edible mushrooms are a good source of protein, which is unusual for a food that is neither a pulse nor an animal product.
after: Mushrooms belong to the fungi, not the plants. They obtain nutrients from organic matter rather than making sugars by photosynthesis. Fresh edible mushrooms contain water, fibre and nutrients, but are not interchangeable with pulses as a protein source. Never taste a wild mushroom to identify it.

before: In 1746, during a voyage, the Scottish physician James Lind made a careful observation. Sailors who were given lemons and oranges recovered. Sailors who were not, did not.
after: In May 1747, James Lind compared six treatments among twelve sailors with scurvy, two sailors per treatment. The pair receiving oranges and lemons improved most rapidly.

before: Notice how much Lind's method matters. He did not guess. He compared two groups of sailors who differed in one respect, and drew a conclusion from the difference. That is an experiment, conducted at sea in 1746, and it saved a great many lives.
after: The comparison supplied evidence favouring citrus fruit over the other treatments tested. It did not identify Vitamin C, and two sailors per treatment is a small sample. More observations and later research were needed to establish the cause.

before: Infer what was happening. The affected regions were not short of food. What they were short of was iodine — and the shortage began in the soil. Where soil is low in iodine, the crops grown in it are low in iodine, and the water is too. People eating a local diet in such a region simply cannot get enough, no matter how much they eat.
after: Iodine deficiency can enlarge the thyroid gland, causing goitre. Diets relying on crops from iodine-poor soil can contribute. But a neck swelling can have other causes: symptoms alone do not diagnose a nutrient deficiency.

before: Iodised salt solves this neatly. Salt is one of the few things that almost every household buys and almost every person eats daily, whatever else is on the plate. Adding a trace of iodine to salt reaches nearly everyone.
after: Iodised salt is a way to supply a small, controlled amount of iodine through a widely used ingredient. This does not mean eating extra salt; it means using iodised salt within the usual limited amount.

before: The people who farm salt In the Little Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, a community called the Agariyas has produced salt for generations. For about eight months each year they live out on the salt flats in extreme desert heat, channelling seawater into shallow pans and working the crystallised salt by hand. The salt in your kitchen has a maker, and the work is punishing.
after: In the Little Rann of Kutch, Agariya salt workers pump underground brine into evaporation pans. Water evaporates and salt crystallises. This example connects a food ingredient to separation by evaporation and to the people who produce it.

before: Look back over everything named so far: carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals. All five are food components that the body actively uses — for energy, for growth, for repair, for defence, for the hundreds of processes that go on without our noticing. Components that do this work are called nutrients.
after: A **nutrient** is a substance the body needs for energy, growth, repair or normal functioning. Carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals are nutrient groups; water is an essential nutrient too.

before: The five major nutrients divide neatly by function: • Energy-giving nutrients — carbohydrates and fats • Body-building nutrients — proteins • Protective nutrients — vitamins and minerals
after: The labels energy-giving, body-building and protective highlight important functions, but the jobs overlap. Proteins can supply energy, fats form parts of cells, and vitamins and minerals support many processes.

before: Vitamins and minerals earn the name protective nutrients because they defend the body against disease and keep it working properly. You need them in tiny quantities, and you need them without fail.
after: Vitamins and minerals help body processes work normally. Calling them protective does not mean that eating one food prevents every disease or treats every symptom.

before: Ira is right on both counts, and there are two more things the body needs that are not nutrients at all.
after: Two further components to consider are dietary fibre and water. Water is an essential nutrient even though it supplies no energy.

before: Roughage, also called dietary fibre, comes mainly from plant foods — whole grains, pulses, fruit with its skin, green leafy vegetables, nuts. Roughage supplies no nutrients whatsoever. The body cannot digest it. That is precisely the point: it gives the digestive system bulk to work against, moving waste through and out. Without enough of it, the gut slows and constipation follows.
after: Dietary fibre, or roughage, comes mainly from plant foods such as whole grains, pulses, fruit and vegetables. Our own digestive enzymes do not break it down, although gut microbes can break down some fibre. Fibre helps bowel function; constipation can have several causes.

before: Water supplies no nutrients either, and nothing works without it. Water carries nutrients from the gut into the blood, carries waste out through sweat and urine, and holds the body's temperature steady. Drink it regularly through the day rather than in one gulp when you are already thirsty.
after: Water dissolves and transports substances, helps remove waste in urine and helps regulate temperature through sweating and evaporation. Needs vary with activity and weather. Water is a nutrient, not a source of food energy.

before: If you want to advise an Indian family on what to eat, you need to know what Indian food actually contains. In the middle of the twentieth century, nobody did.
after: To study diets in India, researchers needed reliable measurements of the foods people ate, along with records of amounts and preparation. A foreign food table could not represent every local ingredient or recipe.

before: Numbers of that kind are hard to ignore, and they changed policy. Gopalan's work fed directly into India's school meal programmes, including the Mid Day Meal Programme launched in 2002 and now run as PM POSHAN, which provides a cooked meal to children in government and government-aided schools. For millions of children it is the most nutritious meal of the day.
after: The national school nutrition programme began in 1995 and developed into the cooked school-meal programme now called PM POSHAN. Nutrition research helped shape school feeding policy. A programme date alone does not prove its effects: those require measurements of children and meals.

before: Open Nutrient Detective on the classroom display. Build a day's meals from the food shelf and watch the nutrient bars fill as you add each item. Try to fill all five bars — then try again spending half as much money.
after: In your notebook, compare two possible lunches using the food groups in this chapter. State what information about portion size and ingredients you would need before comparing nutrient amounts or cost.

before: Before you begin, one habit worth building. Before each test, write down what you expect to happen. That written expectation is a prediction, and it is not a guess — it is your current understanding, put on record where the result can contradict it. A prediction that turns out wrong teaches you more than one that turns out right.
after: Before each test, record what you expect and why. This is a prediction. Keep it beside the observation even if they disagree. Both matching and unexpected results matter; neither alone proves a complete explanation.

before: Read your completed table across the rows, not down the columns. Which foods showed more than one nutrient? Peanut should show both fat and protein. That is the finding that matters most here: a single food usually contains several nutrients at once. Foods are mixtures, not single substances — which is why a varied plate works better than a large one.
after: Read across each row. Which samples gave positive results in more than one test? A food may contain several nutrients. A negative result can mean too little to detect, a preparation problem or a failed reagent: compare with your controls before concluding absence.

before: The wafers carry half again as much energy, five times the fat, roughly a third of the protein and under a third of the fibre. On the numbers, the chana is the better food by a wide margin — and it usually costs less. Foods high in sugar and fat but low in protein, vitamins, minerals and fibre are called junk foods: wafers, candy bars, carbonated drinks and much else sold as a snack. They deliver energy and little else. Eaten often, they crowd better food off the plate and lead to weight gain and the health problems that follow.
after: For these example labels, chana has more protein and fibre and less fat per 100 g. That supports a comparison on those measures, not a universal ranking of foods. Portion size, ingredients and the rest of the diet also matter. Foods high in free sugars, salt or unhealthy fats can displace needed nutrients when eaten frequently.

before: They are coming back, and the reason is nutrition.
after: Compare the grains by named nutrients and growing conditions. A single label such as healthy cannot replace those comparisons.

before: Millets are also easier on the land. They grow in poor soil, tolerate low and unreliable rainfall, and need far less water than rice. In a country where groundwater is falling in many districts, a grain that produces food on a fraction of the water is not a minor advantage.
after: Many millets tolerate relatively dry conditions and can need less irrigation than flooded rice. Water use still depends on crop, yield, climate and farming practice. Compare like growing conditions before making a numerical claim.

before: So a millet does three useful things at once: it feeds a person better than polished rice, it grows where rice will not, and it uses less water doing it.
after: Millets can add variety and nutrients and can suit dry regions. This does not make every millet superior to every rice dish on every measure.

before: The total distance a food item travels from producer to consumer is called its food miles. Shorter food miles are better on three counts. Transport costs money and burns fuel, so a shorter journey means cheaper food and less pollution. Food that travels less arrives fresher. And buying food grown nearby puts money into the hands of farmers near you rather than into transport along the way.
after: Food miles is the distance food travels from producer to consumer. A shorter journey may reduce transport, but total cost, freshness and emissions also depend on farming, storage, transport method and waste. Distance alone cannot establish the best choice.

before: • Food is a mixture of components. The five major nutrients are carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals. Food also supplies roughage and water, which are essential but are not nutrients.
after: • Carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals are nutrient groups studied here. Water is also an essential nutrient. Food supplies dietary fibre as well.

before: • Vitamins and minerals are needed in tiny amounts and are called protective nutrients. Going short of one for long enough causes a specific deficiency disorder — scurvy, rickets, beriberi, goitre, anaemia — each with its own symptoms and its own food remedy.
after: • Lack of a nutrient can cause a deficiency disorder. Symptoms can also have other causes, so medical assessment matters. Examples include Vitamin C deficiency causing scurvy and iodine deficiency contributing to goitre.

before: • Roughage supplies no nutrients and cannot be digested; that is why it works, giving the digestive system bulk to move waste along. Water carries nutrients in, carries waste out, and holds body temperature steady.
after: • Dietary fibre resists digestion by our own enzymes; gut microbes can break down some of it. Fibre helps bowel function. Water transports dissolved substances and helps regulate body temperature.

before: • Food miles are the distance food travels from producer to consumer. Shorter is cheaper, fresher, less polluting, and better for nearby farmers. Wasted food wastes everything that went into producing it.
after: • Food miles measures distance, not total environmental impact. Transport method, farming and storage also matter. Wasted food wastes resources used to produce it.

before: 2. Name the nutrient and the food source you would recommend for each condition. (i) Bleeding gums and slowly healing wounds (ii) Difficulty seeing in dim light (iii) Soft, bent bones in a growing child (iv) Swelling at the front of the neck (v) Weakness and shortness of breath
after: 2. For each condition below, name a deficiency that could contribute and a relevant food source. Explain why symptoms alone cannot diagnose it: bleeding gums; poor vision in dim light; soft bones; neck swelling; weakness.

before: 7. Ira eats biscuits, white bread and noodles, and avoids vegetables and fruit. She often has stomach ache and difficulty passing stool. Which component is missing from her diet? Name three foods she should add, and explain what each will do.
after: 7. Ira records few vegetables, fruits or whole grains in her diary and has difficulty passing stool. Which food component might be low? Suggest sources and state why the diary cannot establish the medical cause of her symptoms.

before: 13. A family lives in a district where the soil is low in iodine. They eat plenty of locally grown food and are not short of meals. Explain why a member of that family might still develop goitre, and what the simplest remedy would be.
after: 13. Explain how iodine-poor soil could contribute to iodine deficiency in a local diet. How does iodised salt help prevent it? Why should a person with neck swelling seek medical assessment rather than diagnose themselves?

before: 16. You are handed an unlabelled solution and told it may be iodine solution. Describe how you would find out, using only what is in your kitchen. State what result would confirm it and what result would rule it out.
after: 16. A teacher provides known iodine solution, starch paste and water. Design positive and negative controls for a starch test. What would a failed positive control mean for a negative food result? Never test or taste an unlabelled chemical.

before: 18. Lind's 1746 comparison of two groups of sailors is described in Case 1. Why was it stronger evidence than one doctor's opinion about lemons? What would have made it stronger still?
after: 18. Lind compared six treatments in 1747, with two sailors per treatment. What does this comparison support? What does it not establish? Explain how a larger, repeated comparison would strengthen the evidence.

before: Carry out this activity under your teacher's guidance.
1. Study Fig. 3.5 until you know the symptoms listed for each nutrient.

2. Talk to people in your neighbourhood — with their permission, and politely. Ask whether they have noticed any of these symptoms in themselves or their family: trouble seeing in dim light, bleeding gums, weakness and breathlessness, aching or bending bones.
3. Where someone reports a symptom, ask — again, politely — what they usually eat. Look for a food group that is largely missing.
4. Correlate the two. Which deficiency would fit the symptoms and the diet together?
5. Suggest which foods, easily available and affordable locally, could help.
6. Always end by suggesting they see a doctor.

A warning that matters. You are not diagnosing anyone. A symptom can have many causes, and only a doctor can test and treat. Your job here is to practise linking evidence to explanation — and then to hand the matter to someone qualified.
A blue-black colour indicates the presence of starch.
Which samples turned blue-black? Compare the result against your predictions. Where you were wrong, say why.
An oily patch that light passes through shows that the food contains fat.
Record your observations in Table 3.3.
A violet colour indicates the presence of protein.
Record your observations in Table 3.3.
